chunks: ʿAlī ibn Muḥammad, from Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, from Mūsā ibn Jaʿfar al-Baghdādī, from Wahb ibn Shādhān, from al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Rabīʿ, from Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq, from Umm Hāniʾ, who said:
I asked Abū Jaʿfar Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī عليه السلام about the saying of Allah, the Exalted:
“But nay! I swear by the retreating ones, the runners, the hiders.”
So he said: “An Imam will go into concealment in the year two hundred and sixty, then he will appear like a meteor, blazing in the dark night.”
“So if you reach his time, your eyes will be gladdened.”

key_terms.إِمَامٌ: the divinely appointed Imam referred to in the narration
key_terms.اللَّيْلَةِ الظَّلْمَاءِ: the dark night; a metaphor for a time of obscurity or trial
key_terms.الْجَوَارِ: those that move along their course; part of the Qur'anic imagery
key_terms.الْخُنَّسِ: the retreating or hidden ones; interpreted here in relation to concealment
key_terms.الْكُنَّسِ: those that withdraw or hide; indicating hiddenness
key_terms.زَمَانَهُ: his time; the period of the Imam’s appearance
key_terms.كَالشِّهَابِ: like a meteor; describing the Imam’s sudden, radiant appearance
key_terms.يَخْنِسُ: goes into concealment or withdraws from open view

ai.seo_question: How do Shia hadith interpret “فَلَا أُقْسِمُ بِالْخُنَّسِ الْجَوَارِ الْكُنَّسِ” in relation to the Imam’s ghaybah (occultation)?
ai.summary: This narration presents the verse as an allusion to an Imam who enters ghaybah (occultation) and later reappears with manifest guidance. It connects the Qur'anic imagery of hidden, moving celestial bodies to the concealed yet divinely appointed Imam, whose advent brings joy to the believers.
